page.title: Proximal particle Langevin — proved results and reference audit
page.heading: Proximal interacting particle Langevin algorithms
page.subtitle: Actual proximal minimizers, corrected MYIPLA, PIPGLA and MYPGD convergence, and a version-specific proof ledger.
page.description: A partial formalization of arXiv:2406.14292v3 with actual-law MYIPLA, PIPGLA and MYPGD bounds, exact Lean proofs, and transparent corrections.
page.status: PARTIAL PAPER FORMALIZATION. Corrected original-center MYIPLA, PIPGLA and MYPGD bounds are proved from primitive assumptions. The exact published constants and several appendix results are not reproduced.
page.source_intro: The attached arXiv:2406.14292v3 PDF is the authoritative reference. Exact local Lean sources are included below; paper claims are distinguished from proved replacements and incomplete results.

intro:
This dedicated page develops proved results related to Cordero Encinar, Crucinio and Akyildiz, Proximal Interacting Particle Langevin Algorithms, arXiv:2406.14292v3. The attached v3 PDF is authoritative; differences from the originally linked v1 are identified explicitly.

The paper is not fully formalized. Genuine original-model bounds for the actual MYIPLA, PIPGLA and MYPGD algorithms are proved, with explicit corrected terms. The PIPGLA result uses a complete alternative stochastic coupling proof, including constructed stationarity and Brownian independence. These are replacements with different rates or constants, rather than claims to reproduce every printed formula. Exact Lean declarations accompany the mathematics, and the final chapter lists the remaining results.

sections.title: What is proved, and what remains open
sections.intro: This page uses the attached version 3 of Proximal Interacting Particle Langevin Algorithms as its authoritative reference. The original request linked version 1; the later supplied PDF supersedes it. Version numbers matter because the PIPGLA target and gradient-scaling calculation changed.

steps.title: A partial formalization of the paper
steps.body:
This is a partial formalization of the paper, with complete proofs of the stated replacement theorems. The development constructs actual proximal minimizers and Moreau envelopes, proves nonasymptotic MYIPLA, PIPGLA and MYPGD bounds for the original nonsmooth marginal maximizer, and derives sharp equilibrium concentration. The actual Gaussian recursions and their finite moments are identified; no final convergence estimate is assumed.

The MYIPLA estimate uses a finite square-root smoothing term instead of the paper’s Taylor-based linear claim. The PIPGLA estimate uses a new synchronous-coupling proof and an explicit conservative constant independent of the time step; it covers arbitrary positive proximal parameters through a proved sensitivity bound. The source’s exact heat-flow proof and numerical formula are not reproduced. Conditional scalar consequences are identified separately from the proved law recurrence.

A corrected W₂ version of the mean-field drift lemma is also proved. MYPGD has a proved finite-particle replacement obtained by an exact Gaussian noise-removal comparison. Continuous L² mean-field equations, a finite smoothing-limit comparison, and an iid particle-limit theorem with uniform timewise L² and one-time W₂ error O(N⁻¹ᐟ²) are also constructed. The source’s exact Appendix B formula, expected path-supremum results and PDE conclusions are not claimed. Every source statement is assigned a status below. A proof gap, a false algebraic identity, and a weaker proved replacement are distinguished.

steps.title: The proved MYIPLA guarantee
steps.body:
Let \(U=g_1+g_2\) on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_x}\). Assume \(g_1\) is differentiable, \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), and has \(L_1\)-Lipschitz gradient. Assume \(g_2\) is finite-valued, convex, bounded below, and \(K\)-Lipschitz. For \(\lambda>0\), set

\[ V_\lambda=g_1+g_2^\lambda,\qquad L_\lambda=L_1+\lambda^{-1}. \]

Take \(N>0\), an initial state with finite second moment, independent standard Gaussian innovations at every coordinate and time, independent of initialization, and

\[ 0<\gamma\le\frac{2}{m+L_\lambda}. \]

Write \(\mu_n\) for the law of the actual scaled MYIPLA state and \(\Pi_{\lambda,N}\) for its continuous Gibbs target. Let \(\theta_\star\) maximize the original latent marginal \(\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}dx\). The formal estimate is

\[ \begin{aligned} \left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2} \le{}&\sqrt{\frac{\lambda K^2}{m}} +\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}\\ &+(1-m\gamma)^n W_2(\mu_0,\Pi_{\lambda,N})\\ &+\frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\lambda}{m} \sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}}\sqrt\gamma. \end{aligned} \]

The target normalization, finite transport moments, stationary reference, and equilibrium concentration are derived through the existing IPLA/ULA development. Neither the displayed convergence bound nor the smoothing bias is an extra assumption. The last term retains its explicit dependence on \(\lambda\); no uniformity in the smoothing scale is asserted. The paper's \(O(\lambda)+O(\lambda^2)\) smoothing expression is replaced by a finite \(O(\sqrt\lambda)\) guarantee, so this is a related proved theorem, not a verbatim reproduction of Theorem 4.1.

sections.title: Start from the actual proximal minimization
sections.intro: The proximity map is constructed, rather than represented by assumed smoothness and residual identities. The finite-valued setting covers the stated globally Lipschitz main-theorem regime; extended-valued indicator constraints from some experiments are not included in this foundation.

steps.title: Existence and uniqueness of the minimizer
steps.body:
For \(\lambda>0\), define

\[ Q_{\lambda,x}(p)=g_2(p)+\frac{\|p-x\|^2}{2\lambda},\qquad P_\lambda(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_p Q_{\lambda,x}(p). \]

A finite-valued convex function on a finite-dimensional real space is continuous. If \(g_2\ge b\), then outside a sufficiently large ball the quadratic term makes \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\) exceed \(Q_{\lambda,x}(x)=g_2(x)\). A continuous function attains its minimum on that closed ball, and the same point therefore minimizes it globally. The proof explicitly constructs a suitable radius from \(\sqrt{2\lambda(g_2(x)-b)}+1\).

The Lean definition chooses a minimizer when one exists and assigns zero outside that domain. All mathematical endpoints establish existence from convexity, the lower bound, and positive \(\lambda\); their conclusions do not depend on that fallback value. Strict convexity of the quadratic, expressed through the variational characterization below, gives uniqueness.

steps.title: The residual is a genuine subgradient
steps.body:
A vector \(s\) is a subgradient of \(g_2\) at \(p\) when \(g_2(p)+\langle s,y-p\rangle\le g_2(y)\) for every \(y\). The exact proximal optimality condition is

\[ p=P_\lambda(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{x-p}{\lambda}\in\partial g_2(p). \]

For necessity, compare the minimizing objective at \(p\) with its value along \(p+t(y-p)\), use convexity, and let positive \(t\) become arbitrarily small. For sufficiency, insert the supporting-hyperplane inequality into the difference of the two quadratic objectives. This proves the global minimum directly, without assuming differentiability of \(g_2\).

Apply monotonicity of subgradients to the residuals at two inputs. It gives firm nonexpansiveness,

\[ \|P_\lambda(x)-P_\lambda(y)\|^2 \le\langle x-y,P_\lambda(x)-P_\lambda(y)\rangle. \]

Cauchy–Schwarz gives nonexpansiveness of \(P_\lambda\). Expanding the square gives nonexpansiveness of \(I-P_\lambda\) as well. Those are derived geometric facts, not premises stored in a proximal-map structure.

sections.title: The Moreau envelope and its proved regularity
sections.intro: Two envelopes must be kept separate. MYIPLA smooths only \(g_2\), giving \(g_1+g_2^\lambda\). PIPULA uses the full envelope \(U^\gamma\). Their convexity and smoothness constants differ.

steps.title: Derive the gradient from two finite inequalities
steps.body:
Define \(g_2^\lambda(x)=Q_{\lambda,x}(P_\lambda(x))\) and \(r_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-P_\lambda(x))\). The subgradient inequality at the actual minimizer proves the lower support bound, while comparison with that same minimizer in the neighboring objective proves the upper bound:

\[ 0\le g_2^\lambda(y)-g_2^\lambda(x) -\langle r_\lambda(x),y-x\rangle \le\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{2\lambda}. \]

The right side is little-o of \(\|y-x\|\), so the envelope is differentiable and \(\nabla g_2^\lambda=r_\lambda\). The global supports imply convexity. Nonexpansiveness of \(I-P_\lambda\) then yields

\[ \|\nabla g_2^\lambda(x)-\nabla g_2^\lambda(y)\| \le\lambda^{-1}\|x-y\|. \]

The gradient is continuous, so the actual envelope is continuously differentiable. This establishes the regularity needed by the existing Langevin theorem even when the original potential has corners.

steps.title: A uniform value gap needs no Taylor expansion
steps.body:
If \(g_2\) is \(K\)-Lipschitz, its subgradient support at a proximal point implies \(\|r_\lambda(x)\|\le K\), and hence \(\|x-P_\lambda(x)\|\le\lambda K\). More importantly, comparing a general displacement with the Lipschitz bound and completing the square gives

\[ 0\le g_2(x)-g_2^\lambda(x)\le\frac{\lambda K^2}{2}. \]

The lower inequality uses proximal optimality at competitor \(x\). For the upper inequality, if \(d=\|P_\lambda(x)-x\|\), then the gap is at most \(Kd-d^2/(2\lambda)\), whose maximum is \(\lambda K^2/2\). This estimate is uniform in \(x\), nonasymptotic, and requires no Hessian or interchange of a Taylor remainder with an integral.

It follows immediately that \(V_\lambda\le U\le V_\lambda+\lambda K^2/2\). This finite inequality supplies the entire smoothing-bias argument in Chapter 6.

sections.title: The particle algorithms are exact coordinate maps
sections.intro: Let \(z=(\theta,x^1/\sqrt N,\ldots,x^N/\sqrt N)\), \(J_i z=(\theta,x^i)\), and \(\mathcal V_\lambda(z)=\sum_iV_\lambda(J_i z)\). All algorithm identities below concern these actual maps and their iterated Gaussian laws.

steps.title: Average the common parameter only after joint proximity
steps.body:
Given any map \(P\) on one joint parameter-particle pair, define its particle action by applying \(P\) separately to each \(J_i z\), averaging the resulting parameter coordinates, and dividing each resulting physical particle coordinate by \(\sqrt N\). The common parameter is not optimized independently for each particle and then kept as \(N\) separate state variables; the averaging is part of the algorithm.

With \(P=P_\lambda\), MYIPLA in v3 equations (9)–(10) is exactly the noisy Euler step for \(V_\lambda=g_1+g_2^\lambda\). Indeed, the pairwise residual-gradient identity gives

\[ \operatorname{Pair}_P(z)=z-\frac\lambda N\nabla\!\left(\sum_i g_2^\lambda(J_i z)\right). \]

Substituting this into the expanded MYIPLA formula cancels the extra multiples of \(z\), leaving

\[ z_{n+1}=z_n-\frac\gamma N\nabla\mathcal V_\lambda(z_n) +\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\,\xi_n. \]

The coordinate proofs also recover parameter noise \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) and physical-particle noise \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\). The full recursion identity follows by induction on the iteration count.

The recursion declarations include the initial and successor identities for each supplied innovation sequence. All pointwise identities concern the explicit state update, before any stochastic convergence theorem is applied.

steps.title: PIPGLA is a different composition
steps.body:
PIPGLA, v3 equations (11)–(14), first takes the noisy smooth \(g_1\) step and then applies the averaged pairwise proximal map. In scaled coordinates it is

\[ y_n=z_n-\frac\gamma N\nabla\!\left(\sum_i g_1(J_i z_n)\right) +\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\xi_n, \qquad z_{n+1}=\operatorname{Pair}_{P_\lambda}(y_n). \]

PIPULA is the special MYIPLA update with \(g_1=0\) and \(\lambda=\gamma\), followed by Gaussian noise. Both distinctions are encoded in separate definitions and proved reduction identities. The PIPGLA proximity step occurs after the noise; its target in the v3 convergence analysis is the original nonsmooth Gibbs model. The MYIPLA theorem cannot be reused merely by renaming this composition.

sections.title: MYIPLA convergence to the smoothed model
sections.intro: The smoothed-model estimate is a theorem about actual Gaussian particle laws. Its proof reuses the existing strong-convexity IPLA development after proving the exact algorithm identity and deriving every required envelope property.

steps.title: Track the smoothing and particle constants
steps.body:
The Moreau envelope is convex. Therefore adding it to the \(m\)-strongly convex function \(g_1\) preserves the constant \(m\). Adding their gradient-Lipschitz estimates gives \(L_\lambda=L_1+1/\lambda\). The replicated-pair identity \(\sum_i\|J_i v\|^2=N\|v\|^2\) then yields lifted strong convexity \(Nm\), lifted smoothness \(NL_\lambda\), and lifted dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\).

Applying the existing Gaussian ULA result at step \(\gamma/N\) produces the contraction \((1-m\gamma)^n\) and the discretization term

\[ \frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\lambda}{m} \sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma. \]

The step condition \(\gamma\le2/(m+L_\lambda)\) is the corresponding scaled ULA condition. Initial finite second moments and Gaussian-law independence are explicit. The continuous reference and finite transport quantities are constructed by the shared theorem, so no convergence estimate or invariant measure is an additional MYIPLA hypothesis.

The law-identification helpers also prove that the actual expanded recursion is probability-valued and that its parameter error about every fixed center belongs to \(L^2\). These guards are used before passing from extended norms to ordinary real square-root integrals in the original-center theorem.

steps.title: The statistical radius has the v3 sharp constant
steps.body:
For a continuous \(a\)-strongly convex potential \(f\) with minimizer \(x_\star\), the new dilation argument proves

\[ \int\|x-x_\star\|^2\,\pi(dx)\le\frac d a, \qquad\pi(dx)\propto e^{-f(x)}dx. \]

The proof uses a sharp radial growth inequality and a change of variables under dilation, rather than assuming an integration-by-parts identity for a nonsmooth density. It therefore applies directly to the continuous strongly convex Gibbs potentials needed here.

The existing Prékopa argument preserves strong convexity when latent variables are integrated out. Raising the marginal density to the \(N\)th power multiplies that modulus by \(N\). Applying the sharp estimate to its actual marginal potential gives

\[ W_2(\Pi_{\lambda,N}^{\theta},\delta_{\theta_{\lambda,\star}}) \le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}. \]

This matches the constant in v3 equation (17) and Lemma A.14. The previous IPLA theorem's \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\) estimate would have been weaker; the new result proves the sharper constant rather than labeling that factor as an error in the paper.

sections.title: Return to the original marginal maximizer
sections.intro: The original statistical model may be nonsmooth. The marginal comparison uses continuity, integrable Gaussian domination from the smooth strongly convex comparison model, and the uniform value gap. Differentiability of the original marginal is not assumed.

steps.title: Integrate the value gap before comparing minimizers
steps.body:
For any potentials \(V\le U\le V+\delta\), exponentiation and integration in the latent variable give

\[ e^{-\delta}k_V(\theta)\le k_U(\theta)\le k_V(\theta), \qquad k_W(\theta)=\int e^{-W(\theta,x)}dx. \]

The smooth strongly convex comparison potential \(V\) supplies positive finite integrals and an integrable Gaussian bound. The original marginal is continuous and decays at infinity; hence it has an actual maximizer. Taking negative logarithms, which is justified by positivity, gives

\[ F_V(\theta)\le F_U(\theta)\le F_V(\theta)+\delta, \qquad F_W=-\log k_W. \]

Let \(\theta_U\) minimize \(F_U\) and \(\theta_V\) minimize the \(m\)-strongly convex \(F_V\). Minimality and the sandwich imply \(F_V(\theta_U)-F_V(\theta_V)\le\delta\). Strong-convexity growth about its minimizer therefore yields

\[ \frac m2\|\theta_U-\theta_V\|^2\le\delta. \]

This argument never differentiates the original marginal and never integrates an asymptotic remainder.

The sharp quadratic-growth lemma uses strong convexity and global minimality, without differentiability of the marginal potential. The comparison model supplies an integrable Gaussian bound for the original weights, giving continuity and existence of an original marginal maximizer by dominated convergence and decay at infinity. Finite positive marginal integrals are established before logarithms and real conversions.

steps.title: Combine a finite center shift with the actual law bound
steps.body:
For the actual split Moreau approximation, \(\delta=\lambda K^2/2\), so

\[ \|\theta_\star-\theta_{\lambda,\star}\| \le\sqrt{\frac{\lambda K^2}{m}}. \]

The original and smoothed marginal maximizers exist under the primitive assumptions. The square-integrable triangle inequality then gives

\[ \left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2} \le\left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_{\lambda,\star}\|^2\right)^{1/2} +\|\theta_{\lambda,\star}-\theta_\star\|. \]

The finite-moment guards are proved before identifying extended norms with real square-root integrals. Substituting the smoothed-model convergence estimate proves the original-center result in Chapter 1.

This is deliberately weaker in smoothing order than Proposition A.1's claimed linear expansion. The formal theorem requires no Hessian along a parameter fiber and no uniform Taylor domination. The weaker order is a change in the formalized result, not a silently omitted term.

sections.title: Full-potential smoothing and PIPULA
sections.intro: The full envelope of a strongly convex potential has a reduced strong-convexity constant. This fact is proved separately from the split-envelope MYIPLA result and clarifies the assumptions in the paper's PIPULA discussion.

steps.title: The strong-convexity modulus changes
steps.body:
If \(U\) is \(m\)-strongly convex, its actual full Moreau envelope is

\[ m_\lambda=\frac{m}{1+m\lambda}\text{-strongly convex}. \]

The proof evaluates the envelope at the convex combination of its two actual proximal minimizers, applies strong convexity to \(U\), and uses the exact square identity for that combination. The remaining comparison is the weighted quadratic inequality

\[ \frac{m}{1+m\lambda}\|v\|^2 \le m\|u\|^2+\frac{\|u-v\|^2}{\lambda}. \]

Completing the square proves this inequality with the displayed sharp modulus. No differentiability of \(U\) is needed. In contrast, smoothing only \(g_2\) preserves the modulus of the unsmoothed \(g_1\); the two constructions must not share a convexity constant by notation alone.

steps.title: What the PIPULA reduction does and does not establish
steps.body:
The algebraic reduction \(g_1=0\), \(\lambda=\gamma\) is proved for the actual update and its full recursion. Together with the envelope theory, it supplies genuine proximity, smoothness, and strong-convexity facts for a full-potential scheme.

It does not reproduce v3 Corollary A.6's original-center finite-time bound. In assumption B1, the displayed proximal inner-product deficit \(\mu\) gives the envelope-gradient constant \(\mu/\gamma\), since the residual is divided by \(\gamma\). The code records that exact implication. A scale-uniform PIPULA discretization theorem and an original-center estimate with the paper's rate remain unproved here; substituting a \(1/\gamma\) smoothness bound into a generic ULA estimate alone would not establish the claimed vanishing error.

A separate proved finite-time result is supplied for the actual PIPULA chain around the maximizer of its smoothed marginal. Assume the original finite-valued potential is \(m\)-strongly convex and bounded below; global Lipschitzness of the strongly convex potential is not imposed. For \(\gamma>0\), its full envelope has modulus \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)\) and gradient Lipschitz constant \(1/\gamma\). The actual proximal/noise recursion equals IPLA for that envelope, and the admissible-step inequality holds automatically. The resulting sharp concentration and Gaussian-chain bound are fully proved. Its conservative discretization term is \((33/20)(1/(\gamma m_\gamma))\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma\), whose coefficient diverges as \(\gamma\downarrow0\). This is not a reproduction of the paper's original-center \(O(\sqrt\gamma)\) convergence rate.

steps.title: Check the literal full-potential Lipschitz specialization
steps.body:
This check is conditional on how the appendix’s reduction is read. If setting \(g_1=0\) also carries A3 onto \(U=g_2\), then \(U\) is globally \(K\)-Lipschitz. Its actual Moreau gradient \(R_\gamma=\gamma^{-1}(I-P_\gamma)\) satisfies \(\|R_\gamma(x)\|\le K\). But B1 with positive deficit gives

\[ \frac{\mu}{\gamma}\|x-y\|^2 \le\langle x-y,R_\gamma(x)-R_\gamma(y)\rangle \le2K\|x-y\|. \]

A nontrivial real Hilbert space contains points at arbitrarily large distance, so these global premises are incompatible. This is kernel-checked for the actual proximal minimizer. If A3 is instead retained for an independent original decomposition \(U=g_1+g_2\), it does not make the full \(U\) Lipschitz; that reading requires its own full-envelope analysis. The result here is therefore a conditional consistency check, not a blanket assertion that Corollary A.6 is false. The separate PIPULA endpoint assumes strong convexity of the full potential and does not impose global Lipschitzness on it.

sections.title: PIPGLA: the deterministic energy bridge
sections.intro: The stochastic argument begins with a genuine inequality for the actual pairwise proximal minimizers. The averaging repair is needed because the lifted proximal identity used in the source is generally false.

steps.title: Prove the nonsmooth energy inequality
steps.body:
Let \(p=P_\lambda(y)\), \(s\in\partial g_2(y)\), and \(a\) be any comparator. Proximal optimality supplies the residual subgradient at \(p\). Combine its support inequality at \(a\) with the support inequality for \(s\) at \(p\), expand the squared distances, and use the nonnegative square \(\|(y-p)-\lambda s\|^2\). The result is v3 Lemma A.8:

\[ \|p-a\|^2\le\|y-a\|^2 -2\lambda\bigl(g_2(y)-g_2(a)\bigr)+\lambda^2\|s\|^2. \]

If \(\|s\|^2\le C\), replace the last term by \(\lambda^2C\). The proof works with any genuine subgradient satisfying that bound; it does not assume an energy estimate or a convergence statement. Taking the minimal section in C1 is one way to supply such a vector.

steps.title: Repair the lifted step using Jensen’s inequality
steps.body:
The roadmap on v3 page 19 identifies averaged pairwise proximity with the proximal map of the lifted averaged potential. Shared parameter coordinates prevent that identity in general. The needed energy conclusion can nevertheless be proved without changing the algorithm.

For arbitrary pair outputs, Jensen's inequality for their averaged parameter gives

\[ \|\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)-a\|^2 \le\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\|P(J_i z)-J_i a\|^2. \]

The scaled latent-coordinate contribution is an exact identity; only the parameter contribution requires an inequality. Apply the single-pair proximal energy result to every summand. Using \(\sum_i\|J_i(z-a)\|^2=N\|z-a\|^2\) and \(G_2=N^{-1}\sum_i g_2\circ J_i\) gives

\[ \|\operatorname{Pair}_{P_\lambda}(z)-a\|^2 \le\|z-a\|^2-2\lambda\bigl(G_2(z)-G_2(a)\bigr)+\lambda^2C. \]

This lifted energy inequality is fully proved for actual minimizers. It repairs the deterministic proof bridge needed in Corollary A.13 while preserving the paper's particle algorithm and its original nonsmooth energy. It is still only one part of the full stochastic convergence proof.

The failure of the lifted-proximal identity has a concrete Lipschitz witness. Take \(N=2\), \(g_2(\theta,x)=|\theta-x|\), smoothing one, common input parameter \(1\) and physical particles \((0,4)\). The genuine pairwise proximal points are \((1/2,1/2)\) and \((2,3)\). Averaging only their parameter components gives \((5/4,1/2,3)\). In the lifted proximal objective with its scaled particle norm, the feasible point \((1,1,3)\) has value \(3/2\), while this pairwise output has value \(51/32\). The strict inequality is kernel checked below. The averaged energy proof above repairs the necessary estimate without this false identity.

steps.title: A genuine stability theorem for the actual PIPGLA chain
steps.body:
The actual averaged pairwise proximal action is nonexpansive in scaled state coordinates. Apply Jensen to the parameter-coordinate difference and keep the latent-coordinate differences exactly; nonexpansiveness of the true pairwise proximal map then gives the state norm inequality. Composing with the sharp smooth forward-step contraction yields, for a common innovation vector,

\[\|T_\gamma(z,\xi)-T_\gamma(w,\xi)\|\le(1-m\gamma)\|z-w\|.\]

sections.title: The stochastic ingredients for actual PIPGLA
sections.intro: This proof concerns the displayed particle algorithm and an actual Brownian Langevin reference. It avoids identifying the averaged proximal map with a lifted proximal map. The final theorem constructs the stationary reference, derives its moments and orthogonality, and takes the infimum over actual couplings; it assumes no convergence estimate.

steps.title: Construct the output laws and retain finite moments
steps.body:
Let \(T_\lambda\) be the actual averaged pairwise proximal map. Write \(F_1=\sum_i g_1(\theta,x_i)\) in scaled coordinates and \(h=\gamma/N\). The recursion is

\[ X_{k+1}=T_\lambda\!\left(X_k-h\nabla F_1(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_k\right). \]

Nonexpansiveness of \(T_\lambda\) and Lipschitzness of the forward drift imply joint measurability and preserve square integrability. The Lean construction first represents every iterate in \(L^2\), then identifies its law with the pointwise recursion. The resulting measure is a probability measure, and its quadratic moments are finite before any extended-real quantity is converted to a real number.

Independent standard Gaussian innovations, independent of the initialization, identify these laws with a canonical Gaussian product-space construction. Two realizations with the same initial law therefore produce the same output laws. These are distributional identities, not convergence assumptions.

steps.title: Bound the reference drift without an inverse smoothing constant
steps.body:
Set \(f=\sum_i g_2(\theta,x_i)\) and \(e_\eta=\sum_i g_2^\eta(\theta,x_i)\). Lipschitzness of the pair potential, Cauchy–Schwarz, and the scaled state norm give

\[ \operatorname{Lip}(f),\operatorname{Lip}(e_\eta)\le NK, \qquad\|\nabla e_\eta\|\le NK, \qquad 0\le f-e_\eta\le \frac{N\eta K^2}{2}. \]

The Moreau envelope has the same value Lipschitz constant as the original potential: translate a minimizing point by the change in input and compare the two quadratic objectives. Its gradient norm is then bounded by that constant. These bounds are uniform in \(\eta>0\), even though the Lipschitz constant of its gradient is \(1/\eta\).

For a smooth strongly convex reference potential \(F_1+e_\eta\), a global minimizer \(z_\eta\) exists and satisfies \(\nabla F_1(z_\eta)=-\nabla e_\eta(z_\eta)\). Sharp Gibbs concentration and the smooth part’s own gradient constant \(L\) yield

\[ \mathbb E_\Pi\|\nabla F_1(Y)\|^2 \le \frac{2L^2D}{m_0}+2K_0^2, \]

where \(m_0\) is the lifted strong-convexity constant and \(K_0\) bounds \(\nabla e_\eta\). Thus the total drift has \(L^2\) norm at most \(G=\sqrt{2L^2D/m_0+2K_0^2}+K_0\), uniformly in the smoothing scale. This is the moment bound needed by the coupling argument; using the full gradient’s inverse-scale smoothness here would lose the useful rate.

steps.title: Derive the needed future-noise orthogonality
steps.body:
A norm bound on Brownian increments alone gives an error of order \(\sqrt h\) at the wrong point in the energy calculation. The proof instead uses causality. At time \(t\), the actual constructed solution is measurable with respect to its initialization and the Brownian coordinates up to \(t\). Future Brownian increments are independent of that history and have zero mean.

\[ \mathbb E\left\langle\nabla e_\eta(Y_t), \sqrt2\,(B_h-B_t)\right\rangle=0, \qquad 0\le t\le h. \]

The development proves the required regrouping of independent families, obtains past/future independence from the Brownian coordinate laws, and transfers it through the actual \(L^2\) representatives. It uses the adaptedness of the constructed integral solution. The displayed orthogonality is therefore derived from the source process, rather than supplied as a premise of a final algorithm theorem.

steps.title: Cancel the nonsmooth energy using the actual integral equation
steps.body:
For a unit-temperature stationary reference \(Y\) with drift \(\nabla(F_1+e)\), share the Brownian increment with the algorithm’s noisy forward step \(S=X-h\nabla F_1(X)+\sqrt2 B_h\). Define

\[ \begin{aligned} v&=(X-h\nabla F_1(X))-(Y_0-h\nabla F_1(Y_0)),\\ R&=\int_0^h[\nabla F_1(Y_t)-\nabla F_1(Y_0)]\,dt, & H&=\int_0^h\nabla e(Y_t)\,dt . \end{aligned} \]

The integral equation gives \(S-Y_h=v+R+H\). The proximal energy inequality and convex supporting planes cancel the original nonsmooth energy against the cross term involving \(H\). Stationarity cancels the expected change in \(e\); a uniform gap \(0\le f-e\le\delta\) contributes \(2h\delta\). Future-noise orthogonality controls the remaining reference cross term by \(2h^2GK_0\).

\[ \|R\|_{L^2}\le Lh\bigl(Gh+\sqrt{2D}\sqrt h\bigr). \]

Weighted Young’s inequality and contraction of the smooth forward step then give the derived one-step estimate

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E\|T(S)-Y_h\|^2 \le{}&(1-m_0h)\mathbb E\|X-Y_0\|^2+\mathcal B(h),\\ \mathcal B(h)={}&\left(1+\frac1{m_0h}\right) \left[Lh\bigl(Gh+\sqrt{2D}\sqrt h\bigr)\right]^2 +2h\delta+2h^2GK_0+h^2K_0^2. \end{aligned} \]

This lemma proves the recurrence from the pointwise energy inequality and integral equation. Its hypotheses include stationarity, moments, and orthogonality; these are discharged by the canonical construction in the next step. It is an alternative synchronous-coupling argument, not a formalization of the paper’s heat-flow entropy proof.

steps.title: Discharge the reference assumptions and take the coupling infimum
steps.body:
For each finite-cost coupling of a current law \(\rho\) and the smoothed Gibbs measure \(\Pi\), append the explicit canonical Brownian probability space independently. The actual integral solution starts from the second coordinate of that coupling. Gibbs stationarity, finite moments, and Brownian orthogonality follow from the proved reference construction.

The noisy forward step from the first coordinate has exactly the prescribed independent Gaussian transition law. The one-step energy lemma therefore bounds the genuine transport cost of the resulting output coupling. The bound is uniform over every finite-cost input coupling. Taking their infimum proves

\[ W_2(\rho_{k+1},\Pi)^2 \le (1-m_0h)W_2(\rho_k,\Pi)^2+\mathcal B(h). \]

No minimizing coupling is assumed to exist. Finite output transport is established before real conversion, and finite moments propagate through the actual chain. This is the missing distinction between a scalar recurrence and a theorem that establishes that recurrence for the algorithm’s laws.

steps.title: Obtain a genuine square-root time-step rate
steps.body:
For \(0 \[ C=\frac{4L^2}{m_0^2}\left(\frac{G^2}{m_0}+2D\right) +\frac{2}{m_0}\left(GK_0+K_0^2\right). \]

To check the bound, square \(Gh+\sqrt{2D}\sqrt h\), use \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\), and use \(h\le1/m_0\). The affine recurrence then gives

\[ W_2(\rho_n,\Pi)^2 \le(1-m_0h)^n W_2(\rho_0,\Pi)^2+hC. \]

For the actual particle chain with equal proximal and forward parameters, set \(\eta=\lambda=\gamma\), \(h=\gamma/N\), \(m_0=Nm\), \(L=NL_1\), and \(K_0=NK\). The true lifted gap is \(N\gamma K^2/2=hK_0^2/2\), so the hypothesis is derived. The reference is the actual smoothed Gibbs measure \(\Pi_{N,\gamma}\). Its moment coefficient \(G\) and the resulting \(C_N\) are finite and independent of \(\gamma\). Hence the proved transport radius is \(O(\sqrt\gamma)\) at fixed dimensions and particle number. This constant is conservative and does not claim the paper’s numerical forcing.

steps.title: Return to the original model and the full parameter range
steps.body:
The actual proximal map obeys a useful parameter-sensitivity estimate:

\[ \|P_\lambda(x)-P_\eta(x)\|\le K|\lambda-\eta|. \]

Indeed, if \(q=P_\eta(x)\) and \(s=(x-q)/\eta\), then \(s\in\partial g_2(q)\), \(\|s\|\le K\), and \(P_\lambda(q+\lambda s)=q\). Nonexpansiveness compares the two inputs. Averaging the parameter coordinates loses no factor of \(N\). Shared-noise contraction then bounds the difference of two actual chains, initialized identically, by \(K|\lambda-\eta|/(m\gamma)\). This pathwise estimate also bounds their parameter RMS difference.

Combine the equal-step law theorem with the proved center shift and sharp concentration. Under the MYIPLA primitive assumptions above, now with \(00\), and \(0<\gamma\le2/(m+L_1)\), the actual PIPGLA algorithm satisfies

\[ \begin{aligned} \left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2} \le{}&\frac{K|\lambda-\gamma|}{m\gamma} +\sqrt{\frac{\gamma K^2}{m}}+\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}\\ &+\sqrt{(1-m\gamma)^n W_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\gamma})^2 +\frac{\gamma}{N}C_N}. \end{aligned} \]

Here \(\theta_\star\) maximizes the original nonsmooth latent marginal, and \(C_N\) is the explicit coefficient in the preceding step. Every occurrence of the smoothing scale and particle number is displayed. For the paper’s corridor \(\gamma\le\lambda\le\gamma/(1-m\gamma)\), with \(m\gamma<1\), the extra term is at most \(K\gamma/(1-m\gamma)\), including the upper endpoint. The resulting bound remains finite there, even though the paper’s printed geometric error-floor formula has a zero denominator at that endpoint.

This is a genuine original-center replacement for Theorem 4.2/A.15 with a different proof and constants. The finite square-root center shift and the conservative coupling coefficient are retained explicitly; the source’s exact formula is not claimed. Its C1 bounded-subgradient assumption implies the Lipschitz hypothesis used here by the proved supporting-plane lemma.

sections.title: The conditional scalar recurrence and the endpoint
sections.intro: The following statements concern a real sequence satisfying an explicitly supplied recurrence. They make no identification of that sequence with a Wasserstein error of actual PIPGLA laws.

steps.title: Retain the correct particle scaling
steps.body:
For the intended squared transport error, the v3 recurrence coefficients are

\[ q=\frac{\lambda(1-m\gamma)}\gamma, \qquad b=\lambda\left(\frac{2\gamma L_1D}{N}+\lambda C\right), \quad D=d_\theta+Nd_x. \]

Only the Gaussian contribution is divided by \(N\). Scaling a gradient by \(N\) scales its squared norm by \(N^2\); version 3 correctly uses this fact in Corollary A.12 and includes \(\lambda NC\) in the numerator before cancellation. The code's scaling certificate is a historical correction to version 1, not a newly discovered error in version 3.

If \(0\le q\) and \(e_{n+1}\le q e_n+b\), induction proves the exact finite sum

\[ e_n\le q^n e_0+b\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j. \]

For \(0\le q<1\), the same result becomes \(e_n\le q^n e_0+b(1-q^n)/(1-q)\), and a nonnegative \(b\) allows the simpler error floor \(b/(1-q)\). These scalar conclusions are proved without assuming the intended algorithm's one-step inequality.

steps.title: A geometric error floor requires strict contraction
steps.body:
When \(0 \[ \lambda<\frac\gamma{1-m\gamma}. \]

The upper endpoint is included with a non-strict inequality in v3 Corollaries A.11–A.13 and Theorem 4.2/A.15. At equality, \(q=1\) and the geometric-series denominator vanishes. A finite-horizon sum remains valid there, yielding the linear bound \(e_n\le e_0+nb\); a finite geometric error floor does not follow.

The Lean statements distinguish those cases explicitly. They also guard positive time step, nonnegative contraction, and positive denominators before division. For \(\lambda=\gamma\), the corrected scalar floor simplifies to \(\gamma(2L_1D/N+C)/m\). This is a consequence of an assumed scalar recurrence, not a completed PIPGLA law estimate.

sections.title: MYPGD: an actual finite-particle replacement
sections.intro: MYPGD retains the latent Langevin noise and removes the common parameter noise. A direct comparison with MYIPLA proves a finite-time theorem for its actual Gaussian recursion. The argument does not require a mean-field convergence assumption.

steps.title: Erase the parameter noise with an actual orthogonal projection
steps.body:
In the scaled particle space, let \(P_\theta\) retain the parameter coordinates and let \(P_x=I-P_\theta\) retain the latent coordinates. These are actual continuous linear maps. For a standard Gaussian vector \(\xi\),

\[ \mathbb E[P_\theta\xi]=0, \qquad \mathbb E\|P_\theta\xi\|^2=d_\theta. \]

For any square-integrable vector \(A\) independent of \(\xi\), expanding the square on the actual product probability space gives

\[ \mathbb E\|A+aP_\theta\xi\|^2 =\mathbb E\|A\|^2+a^2d_\theta. \]

The mixed term vanishes by independence and the proved zero Gaussian mean. This exact identity, rather than a triangle bound on the noise norm, preserves the useful particle-number scaling.

steps.title: Identify the actual latent-noise recursion
steps.body:
Let \(F_\eta=\sum_i(g_1+g_2^\eta)(\theta,x_i)\) in scaled coordinates and \(h=\gamma/N\). The displayed MYPGD step is exactly

\[ X_{k+1}=X_k-h\nabla F_\eta(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,P_x\xi_k. \]

Its common parameter coordinate has no Gaussian perturbation; each physical latent coordinate has the usual \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\) noise. The expanded proximal-residual formula is identified with this gradient step. The pointwise chain is then identified with its measurable Gaussian Markov recursion.

Initialization has finite second moment, and the standard Gaussian vectors are independent across coordinates and times and independent of initialization. The parameter coordinates of those vectors are erased in MYPGD. They remain available as auxiliary noise for the comparison with MYIPLA. No initial iid-particle hypothesis is needed for this weaker finite-particle theorem.

steps.title: Derive the finite-particle comparison cost
steps.body:
The common deterministic smoothed step contracts by \(r=1-m\gamma\) when \(0 \[ W_2(\rho^{\mathrm{PGD}}_{k+1},\rho^{\mathrm{IPLA}}_{k+1})^2 \le r^2 W_2(\rho^{\mathrm{PGD}}_k,\rho^{\mathrm{IPLA}}_k)^2 +\frac{2\gamma d_\theta}{N}. \]

The proof constructs each output coupling, establishes its finite moments, and takes the infimum over input couplings. Starting from the same initial law, \(0\le r<1\) and \(1-r^2=m\gamma(2-m\gamma)\ge m\gamma\) give

\[ W_2(\rho^{\mathrm{PGD}}_n,\rho^{\mathrm{IPLA}}_n)^2 \le\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}. \]

This is a conservative comparison radius, not a claim that removing parameter noise worsens the algorithm. The estimate follows from the two actual recursions and their genuine independent Gaussian transitions.

steps.title: A complete original-center MYPGD theorem
steps.body:
Apply the parameter-projection transport inequality to the two actual laws, then use the proved MYIPLA original-center theorem. With \(L_\eta=L_1+1/\eta\) and the assumptions above,

\[ \begin{aligned} \left(\mathbb E\|\theta^{\mathrm{PGD}}_n-\theta_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2} \le{}&\sqrt{\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}} +\sqrt{\frac{\eta K^2}{m}}+\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}\\ &+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\eta})\\ &+\frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\eta}{m} \sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}}\sqrt\gamma. \end{aligned} \]

Every term is finite under the primitive assumptions, and every law in the statement is the actual defined algorithm law. This is a genuine finite-particle replacement for Appendix B’s Theorem B.1. It has a Gibbs initial-law transient and an explicit conservative comparison term; it does not reproduce the paper’s mean-field metric, constants, or stronger Taylor smoothing expression.

sections.title: Constructed mean-field equations and corrected appendix ingredients
sections.intro: The averaged drift and the continuous L² integral processes are constructed from the actual potential. A smoothing comparison and an exact iid sampling identity are proved. Their norms and initialization assumptions are stated explicitly; pathwise strong-SDE and PDE conclusions are not inferred from L² existence.

steps.title: Control the Bochner expectation by a genuine transport coupling
steps.body:
For a differentiable potential \(V\), define

\[ b_V(\theta,\mu)=\int \nabla_\theta V(\theta,x)\,\mu(dx). \]

Assume \(\nabla V\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(\mu,\nu\) are probability laws with finite second moment. Coordinate projection has norm at most one, so the integrand is Lipschitz and grows at most linearly. Its Bochner expectation is therefore integrable. For any finite-cost coupling, compare its two integrands, apply the norm-of-integral inequality, and use Cauchy–Schwarz. Taking the infimum of actual coupling costs gives

\[ \|b_V(\theta,\mu)-b_V(\theta',\nu)\| \le L\bigl(\|\theta-\theta'\|+W_2(\mu,\nu)\bigr). \]

With the genuine split envelope \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\), the proved constant is \(L_1+1/\eta\). The paper’s \(1/\eta\) constant applies to a full envelope, not to this split expression in general. This is a corrected W₂ version of Lemma C.1: its right-hand side is weaker than the paper’s W₁ statement, and the distinction is explicit. Propositions C.2–C.3 are not consequences formalized by this lemma alone.

steps.title: Construct the mean-field evolution from its actual gradient
steps.body:
On the Hilbert space of square-integrable joint random variables, define the actual drift operator

\[ \mathcal A_V(X)(\omega)= \begin{pmatrix} \mathbb E\nabla_\theta V(X)\\ \nabla_x V(X(\omega)) \end{pmatrix}. \]

The Bochner expectation has operator norm at most one, and both coordinate projections have norm at most one. Thus \(\nabla V\) being \(L\)-Lipschitz implies the conservative bound \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal A_V)\le2L\). Picard iteration in the actual Banach space constructs a continuous L² solution on every finite horizon:

\[ Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal A_V(Y_s)\,ds+B_t^x. \]

Choose a deterministic initial parameter \(\theta_0\), a square-integrable latent initialization, and latent-only Brownian input. The noise is constructed by masking the actual Brownian-coordinate process; its L² continuity and zero initial value follow from the Gaussian laws. The parameter projection is then a constant random variable at every time, giving a deterministic continuous \(\theta_t\). Write \(X_t\) for the latent projection and \(\mu_t\) for its actual pushforward law. The constructed equations are

\[ \begin{aligned} \theta_t&=\theta_0-\int_0^t\int \nabla_\theta V(\theta_s,x)\,\mu_s(dx)\,ds,\\ X_t-X_0&=-\int_0^t\nabla_xV(\theta_s,X_s)\,ds+\sqrt2 B_t. \end{aligned} \]

For \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\), the actual Moreau construction derives the gradient constant \(L_1+1/\eta\). This proves continuous L² integral existence and the displayed parameter/latent identities. It does not establish a pathwise continuous strong-SDE version, adaptedness, or the Fokker–Planck/gradient-flow PDE.

steps.title: A finite smoothing limit without a Taylor remainder
steps.body:
For this result, additionally assume \(g_2\) is differentiable with an \(L_2\)-Lipschitz gradient, while retaining convexity, the lower bound and the global value Lipschitz constant \(K\). The supporting subgradient at a differentiability point must equal the actual gradient. Proximal optimality therefore gives the exact identity

\[ \nabla g_2^\eta(v)=\nabla g_2(P_\eta(v)). \]

Nonexpansiveness of \(P_\eta\) preserves the smooth-score constant \(L_2\), and \(\|v-P_\eta(v)\|\le\eta K\) gives the finite score defect

\[ \|\nabla g_2(v)-\nabla g_2^\eta(v)\|\le\eta L_2K. \]

No asymptotic expansion or integrated remainder is used. If the original sum \(U=g_1+g_2\) is differentiable with \(L_U\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(g_1\) has constant \(L_1\), the component regularity is derived with \(L_2=L_U+L_1\).

The development constructs original and split-smoothed L² integral solutions with the same initialization and additive input. Their input cancels. The actual drift operators differ by at most \(2\eta L_2K\), and their common gradient constant is at most \(L_1+L_2\), independently of \(\eta\). Grönwall gives

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\|Y_t-Z_t\|_{L^2} \le 2\eta L_2K\,\Psi(2(L_1+L_2),T), \qquad \Psi(a,T)=\begin{cases}(e^{aT}-1)/a,&a>0,\\T,&a=0.\end{cases} \]

Specialize the shared initialization to a constant parameter and the shared input to the latent-only Brownian construction to obtain the usual deterministic-parameter mean-field systems. The proved norm is the supremum over time of L² norms. It is not the expectation of a pathwise supremum in Proposition C.3. This is a consistent split-smoothing replacement with explicit assumptions and a finite linear-in-\(\eta\) norm bound.

steps.title: Use actual iid copies for the sampling error
steps.body:
For a square-integrable observable \(\phi\) and a probability law \(\mu\), the finite product measure \(\mu^{\otimes N}\) constructs the independent samples. The proof centers \(\phi\), expands the squared Hilbert norm, and uses independence and zero mean to cancel every off-diagonal inner product. The exact result is

\[ \mathbb E_{\mu^{\otimes N}} \left\|\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi(X_i)-\mathbb E_\mu\phi\right\|^2 =\frac1N\mathbb E_\mu\|\phi-\mathbb E_\mu\phi\|^2. \]

Taking square roots proves the \(N^{-1/2}\) sampling factor. The actual parameter-gradient observable is square integrable under finite-P₂ latent laws, so the formula applies to the mean-field force.

The source’s exchangeability premise alone does not cancel these covariances. A quantitative chaos estimate needs controlled initialization, such as the actual iid construction used here. This exact sampling identity is a proved ingredient; by itself it is not a propagation-of-chaos theorem.

sections.title: Constructed iid particle limit and tagged Wasserstein bound
sections.intro: This is a corrected replacement for Proposition C.2. It constructs the mean-field reference and every finite-particle process from a potential with Lipschitz gradient and an actual iid initialization. Its constant is selected independently of the particle count. The proved process norm is uniform timewise L²; the source’s expected path supremum is not asserted, and the two norms are generally non-comparable.

steps.title: Construct the actual particle equations in physical coordinates
steps.body:
Let \(V\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(\mu\) be any latent probability law with finite second moment, fix a deterministic parameter \(\theta_0\), and take \(T\ge0\). The physical particle state is

\[ H_N=L^2(\Theta)\times\prod_{i=1}^N L^2(X_i),\qquad \|Z\|_{H_N}=\max\{\|\Theta\|_2,\max_i\|X_i\|_2\}. \]

Define the actual particle drift by averaging the parameter force and keeping each latent force:

\[ \mathcal A_N(Z)=\left(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\nabla_\theta V(\Theta,X_i), (\nabla_xV(\Theta,X_i))_{i=1}^N\right). \]

The elementary estimate \(\|(\Delta\Theta,\Delta X_i)\|_2\le\|\Delta\Theta\|_2+\|\Delta X_i\|_2\) gives \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal A_N)\le2L\), independently of \(N>0\). Picard iteration constructs its continuous L² integral solutions. The coordinate identities are proved for the actual gradient functions; choosing this Banach norm does not change the particle recursion or replace its empirical force by an expectation.

steps.title: Couple with genuine independent mean-field copies
steps.body:
Write \(Y_t=(\theta_t,X_t)\) for the constructed mean-field reference on a probability space \(Q\). On the actual finite product \(Q^{\otimes N}\), pull back its latent coordinates through the independent coordinate maps. The parameter remains the same deterministic \(\theta_t\). These bounded linear copy maps commute with the Bochner time integral, so the copied reference satisfies its actual integral equation.

The particle drift applied to these reference copies differs from the copied mean-field drift only in the parameter block:

\[ \delta_N(t)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\nabla_\theta V(\theta_t,X_t^i) -\mathbb E_Q\nabla_\theta V(\theta_t,X_t),\qquad \|\delta_N(t)\|_2= \frac{\|\nabla_\theta V(Y_t)-\mathbb E_Q\nabla_\theta V(Y_t)\|_2}{\sqrt N}. \]

This is an equality derived from the finite-product variance identity. The latent residual is zero. Independence is supplied by the actual product measure, rather than inferred from exchangeability.

steps.title: Construct initialization and all independent Brownian inputs
steps.body:
The base probability space is the product of the specified latent law \(\mu\) and the library’s canonical joint Brownian source. The initial pair is exactly \((\theta_0,X_0)\), with latent law \(\mu\); it has finite second moment and is independent of the complete Brownian paths. On \(Q^{\otimes N}\), the latent Brownian coordinates come from the corresponding independent copies. The parameter Brownian coordinates come from the first copy’s distinct parameter coordinates. An injective coordinate selection proves independence of the complete selected family.

The resulting finite-particle equations are the actual interacting Langevin system

\[ \begin{aligned} \Theta_t^N-\theta_0&=-\int_0^t\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_\theta V(\Theta_s^N,X_s^{i,N})\,ds+\sqrt{2/N}\,B_t^\theta,\\ X_t^{i,N}-X_0^i&=-\int_0^t\nabla_xV(\Theta_s^N,X_s^{i,N})\,ds+\sqrt2 B_t^{x,i}. \end{aligned} \]

The parameter input has the derived exact L² norm \(\sqrt{2d_\theta t/N}\). Hence on \([0,T]\) it is bounded by \(b/\sqrt N\), where \(b=\sqrt{2d_\theta}\sqrt T\). Its continuity and zero initial value are also proved from the actual Brownian laws.

steps.title: Derive a finite-horizon constant before choosing N
steps.body:
The actual centered reference force is a continuous L²-valued function of time. Compactness of \([0,T]\) supplies a finite \(C\ge0\) such that

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\| \nabla_\theta V(Y_t)-\mathbb E_Q\nabla_\theta V(Y_t)\|_2\le C. \]

This \(C\) is chosen before the quantifier over all particle counts; it depends on the reference potential, initial law and horizon, not on \(N\). Subtract the common latent input and the extra parameter Brownian input in the actual integral equations. The proof applies Grönwall to the remaining drift integral, so it never differentiates Brownian noise. Define

\[ \Psi(a,T)=\begin{cases}(e^{aT}-1)/a,&a>0,\\T,&a=0,\end{cases} \qquad C_T=2\big[(C+2Lb)\Psi(2L,T)+b\big]. \]

For every \(N>0\), the theorem constructs the actual particle integral solution with the prescribed iid initialization and proves, for every tagged particle \(i\),

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\left( \|\Theta_t^N-\theta_t\|_2+\|X_t^{i,N}-X_t^i\|_2\right) \le\frac{C_T}{\sqrt N}. \]

For the actual split-smoothed potential \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\), use the derived constant \(L=L_1+1/\eta\). The coefficient can depend on \(\eta\); uniformity in smoothing is not claimed. This is a constructed iid propagation-of-chaos replacement in uniform timewise L² norm. It does not move the time supremum inside the expectation, as in printed Proposition C.2; the expected path-supremum norm controls the uniform timewise L² norm, while the converse need not hold.

steps.title: Pass to the actual one-time laws
steps.body:
The joint pair \((\Theta_t^N,X_t^{i,N})\) has finite second moment, and each reference copy has exactly the actual law of \(Y_t=(\theta_t,X_t)\). Their constructed joint distribution is an admissible coupling. The pair L² norm is at most the sum of its coordinate norms, giving

\[ W_2\!\left(\mathcal L(\Theta_t^N,X_t^{i,N}),\mathcal L(\theta_t,X_t)\right) \le\frac{C_T}{\sqrt N},\qquad 0\le t\le T. \]

The final endpoint retains the particle integral equation, the exact iid initial law and the actual Brownian input alongside this bound. The Wasserstein distance is proved finite before converting it to a real number. This proves convergence of actual tagged one-time laws; pathwise strong-SDE, expected path-supremum and gradient-flow PDE statements remain outside the formalized result.

sections.title: Corrections, qualifications, and coverage of the paper
sections.intro: The reference audit below records proof status statement by statement. Page numbers refer to the supplied v3 PDF. “Replacement” means a different theorem has been proved; “not proved” means no claim of formal coverage is made.

steps.title: A sign error is distinct from an unproved remainder
steps.body:
On page 15, v3 equation (22) prints a negative second-order term in the proximal expansion. Differentiating \(p+\lambda\nabla g_2(p)=x\) gives a positive second derivative contribution. The scalar quadratic supplies an exact certificate:

\[ \operatorname{prox}_{u^2/2}^\lambda(x) =\frac{x}{1+\lambda} =x-\lambda x+\lambda^2x-\frac{\lambda^3x}{1+\lambda}. \]

The negative second-order expression leaves an error at least \(\lambda^2\) when \(x=1\), so it cannot be that quadratic's third-order expansion. This diagnoses the displayed algebra; the quadratic is not globally Lipschitz and is not by itself a counterexample to the full final theorem under A3.

Separately, twice differentiability almost everywhere and the stated moment bound do not supply a uniform integrable third-order remainder. The original \(O(\lambda)\) minimizer claim is therefore not reproduced here. The proved uniform-gap argument replaces it with \(\sqrt{\lambda K^2/m}\). A proof gap does not establish that the stronger conclusion is false.

steps.title: Every theoretical family has an explicit status
steps.body:
MYIPLA, Theorem 4.1/A.5: a genuine original-center replacement is proved, with finite square-root smoothing bias, explicit \(L_1+1/\lambda\) dependence, sharp \(d_\theta/(Nm)\) concentration, and discrete contraction. Proposition A.1’s claimed linear asymptotic expression is not reproduced. The shared library constructs the stationary Langevin reference, but Proposition A.2’s precise strong-SDE formulation is not separately reproduced.

PIPGLA, Theorem 4.2/A.15: an actual original-center law theorem is proved with an independent stochastic-coupling argument, finite moments, canonical Brownian stationarity and orthogonality, and a time-step-independent error coefficient. Positive proximal parameters are covered through the true parameter-sensitivity estimate. Its constants differ from the source. Lemma A.8 and the averaged energy repair are proved; the exact heat-flow entropy/KL route of Lemma A.9/Theorem A.10 and its stated numerical consequences are not formalized.

PIPULA, Corollary A.6: the actual algorithm is identified with ULA for the full envelope, and a separate finite-time smoothed-center estimate is proved. It uses the genuine modulus \(m/(1+m\gamma)\). Its conservative discretization coefficient diverges as \(\gamma\to0\), so it does not establish the paper’s original-center vanishing-bias claim.

MYPGD, Theorem B.1: an actual finite-particle original-center replacement is proved by comparing latent-only and full Gaussian recursions. Its additional radius is √(2dθ/(Nm)); the paper’s mean-field metric and constants are not reproduced.

Mean field: The actual drift integral has a proved W₂ Lipschitz estimate with the corrected split constant \(L_1+1/\eta\); continuous L² mean-field integral equations are constructed, and a linear-in-η uniform L² smoothing comparison is proved. The sharper W₁ metric statement, pathwise expected-supremum versions of C.2/C.3 and PDE conclusions remain unformalized. The actual iid reference and every N-particle process are constructed, with a derived N-independent finite-horizon constant and O(N⁻¹ᐟ²) uniform timewise L² and one-time W₂ comparison. The actual independent Brownian family, initialization and finite moments are retained. C.2 also needs quantitative chaotic initialization; exchangeability alone does not control empirical error at rate \(N^{-1/2}\). The experiment-specific proximal approximations and efficiency claims in Appendices D/E are not certified.

Other source qualifications are recorded rather than silently repaired: restriction of ambient Lebesgue measure to a fixed parameter fiber is zero in positive parameter dimension, so an intended fiberwise condition must use latent Lebesgue measure; convexity gives positive semidefinite Hessians, while the identity-plus-Hessian Jacobian is positive definite; the complexity table cannot be reused without deriving its assumptions and constants for the proved replacement bounds.

Table 1 iteration-count correction: at the fastest admissible choice \(\lambda=\gamma\), Theorem 4.2’s transient is \((1-m\gamma)^{n/2}W_0\). For \(0 \[ n\ge\frac{2\log(W_0/\varepsilon)}{-\log(1-m\gamma)}. \]

Since \(-\log(1-m\gamma)\sim m\gamma\), the count derived from this bound is of order \(\gamma^{-1}\log(1/\varepsilon)\) for fixed nonzero initial error. At the table’s scale \(\gamma\asymp\varepsilon^2/d_x\), it becomes \(d_x(m\varepsilon^2)^{-1}\log(1/\varepsilon)\). The printed essentially logarithmic count omits the inverse-step factor. This calculation concerns what follows from the source theorem; it is neither a Lean-certified complexity theorem nor a lower bound on the actual algorithm’s performance.

closing: The original-center MYIPLA, PIPGLA and MYPGD bounds are genuine theorems about the actual Gaussian recursions. The Moreau construction, stationary reference, finite moments, concentration and stochastic energy recurrence are proved from primitive assumptions. The mean-field development constructs continuous L² equations, a finite smoothing comparison and an actual iid tagged-particle limit. Its uniform timewise L² and one-time W₂ bounds are distinguished from expected path suprema. The reference ledger remains part of the result: algebraic corrections, different constants, weaker replacements, and unformalized appendix statements are visible.
